description:
🗑️ **Reclamation is keyed to a tasklist RUNNING AGAIN, and a merged tasklist never runs again — so its worktree is stranded forever.** Both removal sites assume a next run: `engine/driver.sh:2276` sweeps at worktree CREATION (*"reclaim last run's build artifacts first"*), and `:2652` removes to free the branch for the merge checkout. Neither is reached again once a tasklist merges and retires.

**Measured on cuneiform, 2026-08-21.** `361-run-budget-and-bounce-termination` merged cleanly at `dfe69a08c`, never re-ran, and left **15 GB** standing until it was deleted by hand. It was not alone: `~/.chief/worktrees` had reached **94 GB across 1,867 containers**, of which 1,857 were dead shells and one live container (cuneiform) held 72 GB in six trees of 10–20 GB each. The host sat at **84% full**. Every one of those trees is a full `core/engine/target` — chief creates a worktree per tasklist and they share no build cache, so the cost is per-tasklist-ever-run rather than per-concurrent-run. Running sequentially does not bound it.

**The code already knows this can happen and says so.** `:2652`'s own comment: *"a `git worktree remove` that fails here is what strands a 1.4 GB `target` behind a tasklist that finished cleanly."* The observed strand was ten times that. And the removal is `wt_git remove --force "$wt" 2>/dev/null || true` — failure is discarded at every site, with no retry, no report, and (unlike `:2276`, which follows it with `rm -rf "$wt"`) no fallback on the merge path.

**Two defects, and the second is why the first goes unnoticed.** (1) Nothing reclaims after a successful merge+retire. (2) A removal that loses is silent, so an operator learns about it from `df`, weeks later, rather than from the run that caused it. `sweep_worktree` already tallies reclaimed bytes into `$STATE/sweep.bytes` — the machinery for reporting exists and is not used for the failure case.

userStories.title: A merged tasklist's worktree is reclaimed when it retires
userStories.description: The missing site. Both existing removals assume the tasklist runs again; the one path that guarantees it never will — merge + record + retire — reclaims nothing.
acceptanceCriteria: After a tasklist merges and its record is filed to `completed/`, its worktree directory is removed and the reclaimed byte count is added to the run's existing `$STATE/sweep.bytes` tally, so the run summary can report what a session actually freed

The branch is deleted only when it is genuinely merged — `git branch -d` semantics, never `-D`. A branch that is NOT an ancestor of the base is KEPT and the reason reported: an unmerged branch is somebody's work, and this story must not become a way to lose it
Removal FALLS BACK the way `:2276` already does (`wt_git remove --force` then `rm -rf`), because the merge-path site at `:2652` has no fallback today and that asymmetry is part of why 361 survived

A tasklist that did NOT merge — verify-failed, zone-held, rebase-refused, or left for review — keeps its worktree untouched. Reclaiming one of those would destroy the tree an operator is about to inspect

userStories.title: A removal that loses is REPORTED, at every site
userStories.description: `2>/dev/null || true` at three sites. The failure that stranded 15 GB produced no output at all, so the only symptom was the disk filling weeks later.
acceptanceCriteria: Every `wt_git remove` site reports a failure it could not recover from — naming the path, the measured size, and the reason git gave — instead of discarding it. The existing sweep tally is the natural carrier; a silent strand is the defect

The report is a WARNING and never fails the run: a tasklist that merged correctly must not be marked failed because a directory could not be deleted. The cost of getting this backwards is worse than the leak
A run summary that reclaimed nothing while leaving worktrees behind SAYS SO, with the total still standing — `df` is not an acceptable notification channel for a tool that created the directories

Mutation-check it: make the removal fail unconditionally and confirm the run still completes, still merges, and now reports the strand. A silent failure must be impossible to reintroduce without the test going red

userStories.title: A startup sweep bounds what earlier runs already stranded
userStories.description: US-1 stops the bleeding for future merges; it does nothing about what is already on disk. 1,857 dead containers and 94 GB accumulated before anyone noticed.
acceptanceCriteria: At run start, worktree directories that NO repository references are removed — the verdict computed against every repo that could own one, not just the repo being run. **This is the dangerous part and the acceptance bar is on it:** a first attempt at this analysis checked two repos and classified 1,866 of 1,867 containers as dead, when 29 of them held LIVE worktrees for formant, chief, vita, praxis, talos and others. The check must enumerate live worktrees across all candidate repos and prove it, and the test must include a container that is live for a DIFFERENT repo than the one running
`git worktree prune` runs first in each repo, so a stale REGISTRATION is resolved before any directory is judged by it
A directory is never removed while any live run could own it — a run in a sibling repo must not lose its trees to a sweep started here
The sweep is BOUNDED and reports what it freed, and a `--dry-run`/plan mode prints the verdict set without deleting, so an operator can inspect before trusting it

Deletion logic gets a PURE candidate function with adversarial tests (a path outside the worktree root, a symlink, a name with spaces, an empty string), so "it can never walk outside `$WT_ROOT`" is a property of the code rather than a comment — the `sweep_candidate` convention `cross_system_interop_smoke` already established
